Chapter Eleven: Building a Movement—Solidarity, Strategy, and the Long View
Nobody changes the world on their own, right? The most powerful movements—the ones that really stick—are built on relationships. They're all about trust, about solidarity, and having a shared sense of purpose. And when it comes to the fight for climate justice, it's no different. It takes people from every walk of life, coming together, finding that common ground, and building power from the ground up.
Picture this: a crowded church basement, filled with organizers from all sorts of backgrounds. Some are seasoned veterans of labor struggles, others are brand new to activism. There are disagreements, sure—moments of tension and plenty of uncertainty. But there’s also laughter, music, and this strong sense of belonging. The work? It’s slow. Sometimes it’s pretty frustrating. But underneath it all, there’s this belief that change really is possible.
Most folks never see the hours that go into building those relationships—the quiet acts of care that keep a movement alive. The headlines? They focus on big protests, or a big policy win. But the real work? That happens in kitchens, in living rooms, and in community centers. It’s about listening. It's about learning. And most of all, it's about showing up for each other.
Over time, something becomes clear: strategy matters. Movements that succeed are the ones that know when to compromise, and when it’s time to hold the line. They know when to build alliances, and sometimes, when to go it alone. They’re patient. Persistent. And they're not afraid to learn from failure.
And then there’s the long view. The struggle for climate justice—it’s not a battle that’s won in a single election, or through just one policy fight. It’s a generational project. One that asks for hope, resilience, and a willingness to keep going, even when the odds feel impossible.
So, here’s something worth remembering: movements aren’t just born—they’re made. Built through countless acts of courage, kindness, and a bit of imagination. The work is hard, no doubt about it. But the rewards? They’re profound. A sense of purpose. Real connection. And the possibility of building a better world, together.
